name: Western Ghats (Nilgiri / Silent Valley region)
blurb: Rainforest fruit, shola grassland, macaques, tahr and tigers.

tip.title: Lose the Cullenia flowers
tip.text: Silent Valley's lion-tailed macaques depend on Cullenia flowering. Set Cullenia to -100% and watch the macaque, then the leopard and viper that eat it.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.name: Cullenia
nodes.desc: A tall rainforest tree of Silent Valley. Wikipedia says the lion-tailed macaque's presence there depends on its flowering.

nodes.name: Wild figs
nodes.desc: Fig trees fruit heavily and feed many forest primates, bats and birds. GloBI records macaques and langurs eating banyan figs.

nodes.name: Jamun
nodes.desc: A fruit tree eaten by elephants, macaques and langurs in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Shola grasses
nodes.desc: Frost- and fire-resistant tussock grasses cover the high montane grasslands between the shola forest patches.

nodes.name: Asian elephant
nodes.desc: A megaherbivore that grazes and browses on many plants and eats fruit. The Western Ghats hold the largest wild population in India.

nodes.name: Gaur
nodes.desc: A huge wild ox of Western Ghats forests and hill grassland, living on grasses, herbs and shoots.

nodes.name: Sambar
nodes.desc: A large forest deer that browses and grazes. It is a key prey of tigers and dholes in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Nilgiri tahr
nodes.desc: An endangered mountain goat of the shola-grassland mosaic that grazes grass and small shrubs on rocky slopes.

nodes.name: Lion-tailed macaque
nodes.desc: An endangered omnivore of the rainforest canopy that eats fruit, seeds, flowers and insects, and spreads seeds.

nodes.name: Nilgiri langur
nodes.desc: A leaf- and fruit-eating monkey of the southern Western Ghats; GloBI records langurs eating figs and jamun.

nodes.name: Malabar giant squirrel
nodes.desc: A large canopy squirrel that feeds on fruit, flowers, nuts and bark. Leopards are recorded eating it.

nodes.name: Common crow butterfly
nodes.desc: A common butterfly whose caterpillars feed on fig and other milky-sapped plants, in turn eaten by frogs and birds.

nodes.name: Malabar flying frog
nodes.desc: One of the many endemic tree frogs of the Ghats. It hunts insects at night in wet forest.

nodes.name: Malabar pit viper
nodes.desc: An ambush snake of Ghats forests that takes frogs, lizards and small mammals.

nodes.name: Bengal monitor
nodes.desc: A big lizard that eats insects, frogs, eggs and small animals, and also scavenges carrion.

nodes.name: Dhole
nodes.desc: A pack-hunting wild dog that preys on sambar, muntjac and wild boar in GloBI records.

nodes.name: Tiger
nodes.desc: The top predator of the Ghats forests, taking sambar and gaur, and sometimes elephant calves where ranges overlap.

nodes.name: Leopard
nodes.desc: A flexible hunter that GloBI records eating monkeys, giant squirrels and sambar.

nodes.name: Monsoon rain
nodes.desc: Moist Arabian Sea air is forced up the Ghats and drops heavy rain on the western slopes.

nodes.name: Cold nights & frost
nodes.desc: On the high plateaus frost kills forest seedlings, which helps keep grassland open between shola patches.

nodes.name: Fire
nodes.desc: Periodic fire helps keep montane grassland open, though too much burning shrinks shola forest.

nodes.name: Forest soil
nodes.desc: Nutrient-rich soil under rainforest and shola, kept in place by roots and moist leaf litter.

nodes.name: Fungi, termites & bacteria
nodes.desc: Break down leaf litter and dead animals and return nutrients to the soil.
